21417-forty-six-years-in-the-army:
John M. Schofield, a lieutenant-general of the United States Army, tells his own career in Forty-Six Years in the Army. The book came out in 1897 and opens with his birth at Gerry, New York, in 1831. His father was a Baptist pastor and later a home missionary in the West.

Schofield traces his path from West Point, where he knew General Winfield Scott, through long service. The contents promise chapters on training, command, and the great wars of his time. He offers the book to young citizens whose skill must guard the Union. It is a senior soldier's plain record of a full life.
22095-the-red-cross-girls-with-the-russi:
Margaret Vandercook sent her Red Cross Girls to a new front in The Red Cross Girls with the Russian Army, published in 1916. Her heroines were American girls doing war relief in Europe. In this volume, Eugenia and her friends reach the eastern war. Eugenia risks her liberty, and nearly her life, by hiding a Belgian officer and his family.

With her help the officer wins papers from the enemy and escapes back to King Albert's army. Russian hospitals, refugees, and spies fill the rest of the tale. Vandercook wrote for girl readers who followed the war in the newspapers. The series gave them heroines their own age inside the great events of 1914 to 1918.
22135-the-moral-economy:
Ralph Barton Perry, a young Harvard philosopher, published The Moral Economy in 1909. Perry opens with Bishop Butler's words on provident living. Morality, he argues with Butler, is neither mystery nor mere custom. It is the observance of the laws by which a life is well and wisely spent, like a household run with care.

Perry treats morals as an economy of interests, values, and choices. He asks how competing goods can be ordered without waste of life. The style is clear and argumentative, aimed at students. Perry later won fame as William James's biographer and editor. This early book shows the practical, Jamesian cast of his thought about value and action.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-sain: A 1913 piece on Saint-Remy of Reims, where Clovis was baptized. The font of French kingship stands there. Joseph Dedieu-Barthe tells its tale. France was christened in its church. The holy ampulla was kept in its treasury. Kings were anointed from its sacred oil.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alchemy: This 1913 reference piece on alchemy — the old art of transmutation. Thomas Sloane treats its history and claims. Gold-seekers dreamed in many lands. The Church judged its frauds and hopes. Science's mystical childhood. Its symbols fill the old manuscripts. Its furnaces lit the medieval laboratories.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anatomy: This 1913 reference article on anatomy — the Church and the study of the body. Thomas Merrigan traces the history. Popes favored the dissecting schools. The body reveals the Creator's art. Science in the Church's service. Its study serves the healing art.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-astronomy: This 1913 reference article on astronomy — the science and the Church. Agnes Clerke tells their long alliance. The popes built the observatories. The calendar came from the Church's need. The heavens in the Church's service. Its popes reformed the calendar. Its Vatican observatory watches the stars.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernard-lamy: A 1913 entry on Bernard Lamy — the Oratorian biblical scholar. James Driscoll honors his Apparatus. His Harmony mapped the Gospel story. The French schools knew his zeal. A priest among the exegetes. His Entretiens defended the Scriptures.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blasphemy: This 1913 reference piece on blasphemy — the sin against the Holy Name. John Melody weighs its grave malice. The tongue insults the divine majesty. The law once punished the blasphemer. The sin of the reviling tongue. Its blasphemer was once put to death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-deuteronomy: This 1913 reference article on Deuteronomy — the fifth book of Moses. Anthony Maas unfolds its famous discourses. Moses rehearsed the law's commands. The Shema crowns the Hebrew creed. The second law of the chosen people. Its thirty-four chapters are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-lamy: A 1913 entry on François Lamy — the Benedictine writer. Michael Ott notes his famous works. The entry preserves his modest fame. His pen served the seventeenth century. A monk among the controversialists. His 1711 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-infamy: This 1913 reference article on infamy — the stained repute. Joseph Delany unfolds the canonical kinds. The law brands the guilty name. The courts weigh the seemly proof. The loss of the good fame. Its 1917 Code is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-jacques-: This 1913 reference piece on Barthélemy — the Anacharsis author. Louis Delamarre honors his Greek travels. His pen revived the Athenian age. The Academy prized its learned son. The readers loved his tales. His 1795 death is famed. His 1788 travels are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jerome-bellam: This 1913 reference article on Bellamy — an English writer of note. Thomas Taaffe surveys his works. Little is known of his career. The seventeenth century was his era. The learned press knew his pen. His 1690 works are famed. His 1690 writings are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-political-eco: Political economy is the science of wealth and its laws. This entry examines its schools, from Smith to the present, and the Catholic view. The dismal science, judged: its cold Manchester school meets the Church's warm and human answer at last.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-french-ac: The French Academy is the forty immortals. This long entry examines its Richelieu, its dictionary, and its fame. The guardian of the French tongue: their great dictionary crowned Paris in the 1630s of the Richelieu in the very old palace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-joseph: Lamy was the orientalist of Louvain. This long entry examines his 1800s, his Syriac, and his works. The scholar of the Eastern texts: his learned Syriac crowned Louvain in the 1880s of the university in the truly very old faculty.
cobb-s-anatomy: Irvin S. Cobb's 1912 humor book dissecting the human body, Southern-style: each organ gets a comic lecture full of tall tales and homespun wisdom. Cobb was one of America's highest-paid humorists, and this shows why. Folksy, funny, and packed with period charm.
dear-enemy: Webster's 1915 Dear Enemy letters follow Sallie McBride running an orphanage. Love writes. The Tower library holds the full text. It penned care. Orphans grew. Letters flew. Hearts warmed. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
doe-osti-2571755-data-structure-alchemy: Database researcher Stratos Idreos lays out a fresh way of thinking about data structures, the building blocks that decide how software stores and retrieves information. The report argues that old categories for these structures no longer fit how modern systems actually work. Readers get a new map for designing storage that runs faster and scales better.
doe-osti-3021282-plant-design-for-a-deve: Bioeconomy plants got design-workshopped, and this DOE text covers frontier science. The pages detail the report findings. The bio folks get their data. The series was workshop. The data were bio. The science was frontier. The workshop was series.
govdocs-archive_org-the-christ-myth-titl: Arthur Drews argued in The Christ Myth, published in 1909, that Jesus never existed as a historical person. Only the title page of the work is described in the record held here. Drews, a German philosopher, claimed the Christ figure grew from older myths and cults. His book caused a public storm in Germany and still anchors the Christ myth debate. The title page alone marks that famous and fought-over work.
jeremy: Hugh Walpole’s Jeremy tells a beloved boyhood tale. The young hero’s world comes alive. Tender scenes capture childhood’s magic. A classic for boys of all ages, Walpole, boyhood, Hugh Walpole, childhood, tale.
last-enemy:
H. Beam Piper's story Last Enemy first ran in Astounding Science Fiction in August 1950. A note warns that its last enemy was the toughest of all. Winning against him carried its own danger.

The tale opens at a U-shaped dinner table as talk dies down. Soft music drifts over the guests. Behind that calm sits a society shaped by strange beliefs. In that world, killing can count as an honorable profession. Piper builds science fiction from that single unsettling custom and its effects. The dinner scene's calm opening makes later dangers hit harder. Piper often built stories around one strange social rule.
personal-memoirs-of-p-h-sheridan-general:
Philip Henry Sheridan finished his Personal Memoirs in August 1888, dedicating them to his comrades in arms during the War of the Rebellion. In his preface he owns the difficulty of telling his share in great events without giving his own acts unmerited prominence. He claims no literary merit, only the importance of his subject.

The complete memoirs open with his Irish parents, who came from County Cavan to America in 1830. Sheridan tells of grocery clerking, West Point, a fistfight, suspension, and graduation. From such beginnings he rose to command the Union cavalry and become one of the war's famous generals.
pocket-lavater-physiognomy:
Two sages' face lore is shrunk for the coat in The Pocket Lavater, an English digest of near 1800. Johann Caspar Lavater's great work on the face had made face lore a craze in the West. Della Porta's old beast lore stands back of it. The digest picks the best rules, signs, and draws from both and binds them in a small, cheap book for the crowd.

A clerk could learn to read a brow, nose, or chin on his walk to work. The science was false, yet the fad was vast. The book is that fad in brief.
podcast-joerogan-QwfJIFH3WMY:
Travis Walton retells his encounter with aliens in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience. Walton's 1975 case, in which a logging crew reported a craft and Walton vanished for five days, was made into the film Fire in the Sky. He has told the story for decades, and it has not softened.

He goes over the night in the forest, the missing days, and the storm of tests and doubts that followed. Rogan asks what he remembers clearly and what remains blank. The segment adds a fresh telling of a foundational abduction case, in the voice of the man at its center.
podcast-tuckercarlson-61rCf7INomY:
Former CIA officer Bernard Hudson joins Tucker Carlson to discuss the Las Vegas Cybertruck explosion, the New Orleans truck attack, and agency corruption. Both attacks struck around New Year's Day and raised hard questions about warning signs. Hudson reads them with an operator's eye.

Hudson gives his view of what investigators may have missed in each case. He also addresses Tulsi Gabbard's move into the intelligence leadership and what it could change. Carlson presses him on how deep the rot inside the agencies runs. Watching viewers get an insider's take on a chaotic stretch of news.
prisoner-for-blasphemy:
George William Foote told the story of his own prosecution in a book first printed in London in 1886 by the Progressive Publishing Company. Foote, a freethought writer, was charged with blasphemy and tried more than once for what he had published.

Chapters follow the summons, the indictment, and trials at the Old Bailey, then take the reader inside Newgate and Holloway Gaol. Prison life, a prison chaplain, and the gains and losses of the fight fill the closing pages. Readers get a first-hand record of a famous Victorian free-speech case.
speculations-from-political-economy:
C. B. Clarke offers nine short pieces in Speculations from Political Economy, and warns that they are guesses, by no means all plans he backs. Near all grew, he says, from weighing plain claims of the science of trade and wealth. Some are old, or came from friends; some, he thinks, are new, and many will call the new ones unpractical, that being the approved word for an idea new to them.

His heads run from the yield of labor and trade answers and strikes back, through world free trade and the ransom of the land. Making the most of our land, free trade in railways, land law reform, the leveling of taxes, and the wealth of the nation close the set. The first piece takes up the yield of labor, a point Clarke says trade writers have rated too low, on cases drawn from Edward Wilson.
taken-by-the-enemy:
Taken by the Enemy opens The Blue and the Gray series. Oliver Optic wrote the series for boys. Lee and Shepard of Boston issued it. Each volume cost a dollar and a half. The publisher's list at the front divides the series into Afloat and On Land sets.

The Afloat set runs from Taken by the Enemy through Within the Enemy's Lines, On the Blockade, and Stand by the Union to Fighting for the Right and A Victorious Union. A frontispiece caption gives three cheers for Captain Passford, the series hero. Optic wrote swift, patriotic sea and war adventures in which young Union men prove themselves under fire, and this first volume launches Passford's career.
tanakh-jps-1917-deuteronomy:
Deuteronomy, the fifth book of the Torah, appears here in the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 English version of the Holy Scriptures. The book is framed as words Moses spoke to all Israel beyond the Jordan, late in the long desert march.

Moses recalls how God spoke at Horeb and urged the people to move on and take the promised land. He dates his speech to the fortieth year, after the fall of Sihon and Og, kings east of the river. Readers get law retold as a last charge, with past mercy, fresh commands, and the land set plain before a new age group poised to enter it.
the-amateur-army: Front matter alone is present for Patrick MacGill's The Amateur Army, a London book from Herbert Jenkins dated 1915 in Roman numerals. A frontispiece names its author Rifleman Patrick MacGill, and earlier works listed are Children of the Dead End and The Rat-Pit. The contents map a new soldier's first months: enlisting and being billeted, rations and sick parade, pickets and special leave, officers and rifles, a coffee-shop, and the night side of soldiering.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-5-deut:
Deuteronomy , read in the King James Version, begins with words Moses spoke to all Israel on this side of the Jordan, in a wilderness plain facing the Red Sea. Places named include Paran, Tophel, Laban, Hazeroth, and Dizahab.

A note gives eleven days' journey from Horeb to Kadeshbarnea. In the fortieth year, in the eleventh month, Moses speaks all God commanded him, after defeating Sihon of the Amorites and Og of Bashan. On this side Jordan, in Moab, Moses begins to declare the law, recalling what God spoke at Horeb. A final address, not a new conquest, opens the book.
the-boy-allies-at-verdun-or-saving-franc:
Clair W. Hayes wrote The Boy Allies at Verdun, or Saving France from the Enemy, dated 1917. The first chapter is called The Eve of Verdun. Its date is February 22, 1916, and its hour is close to six at night.

A car speeds north along the French line, which for close to two years has held back the German hosts. For months the two sides have fought to a draw from the North Sea to the Swiss line. Now the hour nears for the start of the most harsh and wasteful fight of the war so far. At the wheel sits Hal Paine, an American youth of some eighteen years, in the dress of a British horse officer. Two riders in the back seat bounce and talk as the car leaps the rough road.
the-colored-regulars-in-the-united-state:
Chaplain T. G. Steward, D.D., of the Twenty-fifth U.S. Infantry, wrote this history of Black soldiers in the United States Army. The A.M.E. Book Concern published it at Philadelphia in 1904. An introductory letter from Lieutenant-General Nelson A. Miles, commanding the Army, stands at its front.

The full title promises a sketch of the history of the colored American, plus an account of his services in the country's wars. That account runs from the Revolutionary War to 1899. Chapter I sketches social history: the importation of the Africans, the character of the colored population in 1860, and free colored people in the South and the North. Chapter II takes up the military spirit, from early literature of Negro soldiers through the Revolution, the War of 1812, and Negro troops in the Civil War. Steward writes as both chaplain and historian of his own regiments' tradition.
the-future-of-astronomy:
Edward C. Pickering, head of the Harvard College Observatory, gave this talk on the future of astronomy in 1909, first printed in the Popular Science Monthly. He asks why star study draws such rich support.

Pickering notes that observatories hold endowments near half a million dollars a year, while physics, rich in trade uses like the telephone and cable, gets far less. He asked the wisest man he knew, who said astronomy fires the imagination. Vast distances and hard puzzles draw men who made fortunes in mills and counting rooms. Pickering then maps how star study should be run and shared in the years ahead.
the-governess-or-the-little-female-acade:
Sarah Fielding wrote The Governess. Its subtitle is Or, The Little Female Academy. Its heading is dated 1749. The tale opens in the north of England. A gentlewoman takes up the schooling of young ladies there. She teaches reading, writing, needlework, and proper behavior. Her chief aim is to improve their minds in useful knowledge.

The governess is Mrs. Teachum, a clergyman's widow. She lived nine years with her husband in full accord. The pair planned with great care the education of their two little girls. Mr. Teachum loved to improve his wife by talk. One of his constant themes was the education of children. That training, cut short by his last illness, shapes the school she now runs. Her girls are to be obedient to their elders. They are to be gentle, kind, and warm to each other.
the-green-mummy: Fergus Hume wrote The Green Mummy. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a contents list of twenty-one chapters. The heads open with The Lovers and Professor Braddock. They name A Mysterious Tomb, The Unexpected, and Mystery. They name The Inquest and The Captain of The Diver. They name Mrs. Jasher's Luck and The Don and His Daughter. They name The Manuscript, A Discovery, and More Mystery. They end with A Story of the Past. No chapter text is present.
the-intrusion-of-jimmy:
P. G. Wodehouse opens this novel at the Strollers' Club. The main smoking-room has filled for half an hour. Chapter I is titled Jimmy Makes a Bet. The contents promise thirty chapters of house-party comedy. Pyramus and Thisbe come early. Mr. McEachern and Molly follow. A thief in the night appears. An exhibition performance and a move to Dreever come next. Jimmy adopts a lame dog. A marriage is arranged along the way.

Wodehouse calls the Strollers' the pleasantest club, not the grandest. A young gentleman hero moves among its members. Policemen's daughters, crooks, and earls cross his path. Later headings promise loathsome gifts and family jars. A treasure-seeker and explanations follow. Stirring times await Sir Thomas. The machinery is classic early Wodehouse. A bet starts everything. An assumed errand and a great house do the rest.
the-physiology-of-taste-or-transcendenta: Brillat Savarin's The Physiology of Taste bears the subtitle Transcendental Gastronomy. Fayette Robinson translated it from the last Paris edition. Here only the title page and contents appear, so the meditations themselves are absent. The contents list short sayings by the professor, a talk between the author and his friend, a life of the author, and a preface. Numbered meditations then start with the senses and move on to taste itself.
the-uses-of-astronomy:
Edward Everett delivered The Uses of Astronomy at Albany on August 28, 1856, for the inauguration of the Dudley Astronomical Observatory. Ross and Tousey published the oration in New York the same year. The pamphlet pairs the speech with a condensed report of the proceedings and an account of dedicating New York State Geological Hall.

An explanatory note says newspaper editions of the record were exhausted within a month. The publisher hopes wide circulation of both ceremonies will benefit the cause of science in the public mind. Everett, a distinguished statesman, is praised for investing astronomy with new beauties in one of his most brilliant compositions. Demand, not profit, is offered as the motive for reprinting.
the-war-romance-of-the-salvation-army:
Evangeline Booth, commander-in-chief of the Salvation Army in America, wrote The War Romance of the Salvation Army with Grace Livingston Hill. J. T. Lippincott copyrighted the volume in 1919. Portraits show General William Bramwell Booth and Evangeline Booth herself before the narrative begins.

Her foreword answers a generous public's insistent call for an account of the Army's work during the world conflict for liberty. Service is the watchword, she writes, and no reward equals doing the most good to the most people in the most need. The Army held itself ready as American forces gathered, entered France ahead of the Expeditionary Forces, and meant to stay until the last troops came home.
the-world-english-bible-web-deuteronomy:
Book five of the World English Bible, Deuteronomy, records words Moses spoke beyond the Jordan. Israel camps in the wilderness near Suph and Paran. The timing is precise: the fortieth year, the eleventh month. Moses speaks after defeating Kings Sihon and Og. In Moab he begins declaring the law. He recalls God's command at Horeb to move on.

The people had stayed long enough at that mountain. Their journey toward the Amorites' hill country lay ahead. Deuteronomy retells the law for a new generation. Covenant loyalty shapes every speech in it. Readers meet Moses as teacher on the border of the promised land.
thirteen-months-in-the-rebel-army: William G. Stevenson is named in brackets as author of Thirteen Months in the Rebel Army, published in New York in 1862. The subtitle calls him an impressed New Yorker, meaning a man forced into service. His narrative covers infantry, ordnance, cavalry, courier, and hospital services. The title page also promises an exhibition of the power, purposes, and military despotism of the South. A frontispiece shows a council of war before Pittsburg Landing. What is present here stops at the front pages, so Stevenson's adventures themselves do not appear.
vedas-catholic-encyclopedia-remy:
Arthur Remy wrote the Catholic Encyclopedia entry on the Vedas, the oldest scriptures of Hinduism. The encyclopedia aimed to give Catholic readers sound learning on all faiths. Remy's article treats a vast subject in compact form.

He outlines the four Vedas and their hymns, prayers, and rites. He notes their age, language, and place in Indian worship. His tone is scholarly, if dated in places. The entry shows how the Church once taught its flock about a far faith. It suits readers who compare religions and want the period view stated plainly.
